aurora-station.story:
Aurora Station was a proposed hotel in orbit from Orion Span, a startup led by the former software engineer Frank Bunger, which assembled its module in Houston, Texas, and developed its software in the San Francisco Bay Area. Announced in April 2018 at the Space 2.0 Summit in San Jose, California, it was to be a single module 14 feet wide, with its length given as 35 feet in some reports and 43.5 feet in others, about as roomy inside as a Gulfstream G550 business jet, circling 200 miles above Earth with four guests and two crew.

The offer was to sell the experience of being an astronaut. A 12-day stay would cost $9.5 million per person, or about $790,000 a night, and a refundable $80,000 deposit held a place. Guests would see 384 sunrises and sunsets on the trip. Launch was planned for late 2021, with guests the following year. The company said its top technical staff came from NASA, but it would not say how much money it needed. It signed no launch contract and never started construction.

An archived copy of its website said in March 2021 that operations had stopped and deposits had been refunded, while a later radio report gave 2022 as the year it closed. The company never claimed sovereignty, and it shut down before any regulator had to decide who would govern guests on board. Had it flown, an American company would have needed American authorisation and supervision, under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. The obstacle that ended it was money, well before the law on private hotels in orbit came into play.
aurora-station.why: Length conflict: GeekWire gives 43.5 ft and Wikipedia 44 ft against the 35 ft stated flatly. Houston base was too simple: GeekWire places assembly in Houston and software in the Bay Area, and Wikipedia calls it a California startup. Wikipedia's 5 March 2018 announcement date was not adopted, because 2018 press is dated April.

add_sources.t: Looking for a space hotel? Orion Span says it'll put one in orbit by 2022, GeekWire

cloud-constellation-spacebelt.story:
SpaceBelt was a plan by Cloud Constellation Corporation of Los Angeles to store customers' data on satellites in low Earth orbit and pass it between them, so that it never crossed the public internet or any country's land networks. It would use a ring of 10 satellites, 650 to 700 kilometres up in a low orbit close to the equator, linked by lasers and reached from the ground through small dish terminals. This would make it an orbital data haven, a place to keep information out of reach of national rules.

The company was founded in 2015. Its marketing said it would sidestep laws on how data moves between countries. Its president Cliff Beek pitched hosting data without wrangling over international compliance, and in 2017 the company offered it as an answer to GDPR, the European Union's data protection rules. Trade reporters pointed out that those rules protect European residents' data even when it is processed outside the EU, so moving the data does not remove the duty.

The legal claim has a further weakness. Under the Outer Space Treaty, the launching and registering country keeps legal authority over a satellite and answers for what its companies do there. An American company with customers on the ground would remain within reach of courts and regulators, through the company itself and through its terminals.

The money problem came first. The company raised $5 million in 2016 and said it needed $480 million to reach orbit. In December 2018 it announced a $100 million commitment from HCH Group of Hong Kong. In November 2019 CFIUS, the US panel that reviews foreign investment, raised problems with that money because HCH is a Chinese company. So a US government panel stood in the way of the funding for a project pitched as beyond national rules. By April 2020 no replacement funding had been announced, and that month the company announced a benchmark test with IBM, with service planned for 2022. Launch plans changed along with the design. A September 2017 agreement with Virgin Orbit was overtaken when a redesign made the satellites too large for its rocket. LeoStella was chosen in May 2019 to build them, and a single launch on a European Vega-C rocket from Kourou was planned for 2024. No launch has been reported, and a space industry directory updated in September 2025 still listed no announced first launch.
cloud-constellation-spacebelt.why: Altitude was a range and the orbit low-inclination. Added the missing launch history and a September 2025 status, replacing 'no news since 2020'.

kessler-limits.story:
Kessler syndrome is a predicted chain reaction of collisions in orbit, and it places a physical limit on any plan to live or build there. In June 1978 the NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais published a paper called "Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt". Kessler and Cour-Palais showed that if low Earth orbit became crowded enough, collisions would create debris, and that debris would cause more collisions, without anyone launching anything further.

Kessler reached this by applying to satellite records a method developed for studying the asteroid belt. He found that 42 percent of catalogued debris came from 19 events, mainly explosions of spent rocket stages when leftover fuel burst their tanks. At the time many people thought drag from the thin upper atmosphere would clear debris faster than it formed. In 2009 Kessler wrote that modelling showed the environment had already become unstable, so that fragments from future collisions would pile up faster than drag could remove them, even with no new debris sources. By 2025 there were an estimated 11,800 satellites in orbit, of which 7,135 belonged to Starlink, and the chain reaction becomes likelier as the number grows.

This bears on any claim to a place in orbit, because a settlement cannot fence off its surroundings. One operator's debris endangers all the others. A would-be orbital nation would depend on the conduct of every operator around it and would have no power over them.

No treaty sets a limit on debris, so the rules are national. On 29 September 2022 the US Federal Communications Commission voted 4-0 to require operators of satellites in low Earth orbit to bring them down as soon as practicable and no later than five years after the end of their mission, replacing a long-standing recommended practice of 25 years. Its 2023 fine against Dish Network is an early case of one country enforcing its own debris rules. In the worst case, some orbital regions would become unusable for many generations.
kessler-limits.why: The five-year rule was stated for all satellites; it covers low Earth orbit. Added date, vote and the earlier 25-year practice.

add_sources.t: FCC Adopts 5-Year Rule for Deorbiting Satellites, Via Satellite

republic-of-uzupis.story:
Užupis is a neighbourhood of less than one square kilometre in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, that artists declared an independent republic as a local celebration. Its name means beyond the river, because it lies on the far side of the Vilnele river, and a bridge marks the way in. Around 7,000 people live there, about 1,000 of them artists. Under Soviet rule the district was derelict and dangerous. One main road was called the Street of Death, for its crime and for the Jewish population destroyed in the Holocaust.

When the Soviet Union fell in the early 1990s, many plinths across Vilnius stood empty after their statues were removed. In 1995 local artists used one for a statue of the American musician Frank Zappa, who had never been there, as a symbol of freedom. Two years later, on 1 April 1997, April Fools' Day, they went further and declared the district independent, although some accounts give 1998. A founder, Tomas Čepaitis, later cited the old idea that a good country should have no more than about 5,000 citizens, small enough that everyone knows everyone and cheating is hard.

The republic has a president, Romas Lileikis, a government with foreign and tourism ministers, its own unofficial currency, and a navy of three or four small boats used for ceremonies. An army of about 10 men has been retired. Its flag shows a hand with a hole in the palm, unable to hold a bribe, and the hand's colour changes with the seasons, blue in winter, green in spring, yellow in summer and red in autumn. The border goes unguarded except on Užupis Day, 1 April, when visitors can have their passports stamped on the bridge.

Lileikis and Čepaitis wrote the constitution in about three hours one afternoon in 1998, after Lileikis came round to take a bath because he had no hot water. That is why its clauses, counted as 41 in some accounts and 38 in others, include a right to hot water, heating in winter and a tiled roof, along with lines such as "a dog has a right to be a dog". The text is displayed on mirrored plates along a road called the Avenue of Constitutions, in more than 30 languages by one count and 23 by another.

Foreign governments do not recognise Užupis, and no dispute with the Lithuanian state is reported. Residents remain Lithuanian citizens under Lithuanian law, and the republic has become a source of pride in Vilnius. The Dalai Lama, made an honorary citizen, visited in 2013 and 2018, and Pope Francis blessed the constitution during his visit to Vilnius in September 2018. The state can treat it as local culture at no cost, because the claim takes nothing from the state's law or taxes.
republic-of-uzupis.why: Wikipedia conflicts on the year in its own text (1997 infobox, 1998 body), and gives 38 articles, 23 languages and a seasonal flag colour. Each was stated flatly here. Added the Dalai Lama and papal visits. The listed Wikipedia URL does not resolve; the replacement does.

republic-of-vevcani.story:
Vevčani is a village of about 2,400 people near Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia, in the Jablanica Mountains along the border with Albania, that has tried independence more than once. Its isolated terrain let it keep its own habits under the Ottoman Empire and communist Yugoslavia, including its Orthodox religion, a Slavic dialect found nowhere else, and a January carnival said to be 1,400 years old.

The first clash was over water. The Vevčani springs are at the centre of the village's celebrations. In May 1987 the Yugoslav government planned to divert the spring water to new villas by Lake Ohrid for the communist elite. Villagers spent the summer building barricades and threatening to secede. Special police with batons were sent in during what became known as the Vevčani Emergency, which lasted three months, and the government then backed down. Protests over the arrests and injuries continued on and off in Skopje and Belgrade for four years.

When Yugoslavia broke up, the republics that made up the federation each held referendums. Macedonia declared independence on 8 September 1991. On 19 September the village declared itself an independent republic as well, with only 36 of about 2,000 voters against. Macedonia never recognised this, but its government was also dealing with armed separatists in ethnic Albanian areas and was prepared to make a local concession. It let Vevčani separate from the larger Struga municipality and form its own municipality, which still exists. Accounts differ on the date. One gives 1994 and another gives 2002, and a report from January 2002 already describes the village as having a mayor. So the bid won a legal result, in the form of ordinary local government inside the new state.

In 2002 locals revived the republic as a light-hearted way to draw tourists and poke fun at politics. They fly a flag beside the national one at the municipal building, and they sell red passports with dated entry stamps at souvenir stands, along with their own printed money. North Macedonia governs the village as part of its territory. The real gain from the secession came from the municipal status, while the passports and banknotes that came later bring in tourists and have no legal effect.
republic-of-vevcani.why: The 1994 date is disputed: Wikipedia's Republic article says 1994 and its village article says the municipality was reconstituted in 2002.

add_sources.t: Article on Vevcani dated 6 January 2002, Global Policy Forum archive

swarm-spacebees-fcc.story:
Swarm Technologies is an American satellite company founded in 2016 by Sara Spangelo and Benjamin Longmier, and it launched its first satellites without permission. The company used very small satellites, each a quarter of the smallest standard size, known as 0.25U. Their small size was the source of the dispute.

In April 2017 it asked the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for an experimental licence to run four such satellites, called SpaceBEEs, and two ground stations. In December 2017 the FCC refused, because it feared satellites so small could not be tracked and could become invisible debris. Swarm launched them anyway on 12 January 2018, on an Indian rocket that also carried other satellites.

The launch was on foreign soil, which might suggest the FCC had no say. But the agency reached the company by other routes. Swarm was an American company, and its satellites had sent signals to ground stations in Georgia in the United States for more than a week. The agency also found unauthorised tests from weather balloons. After reports of the launch surfaced, it opened an investigation in March 2018 and warned the whole industry not to arrange launches after a licence had been refused.

In December 2018 Swarm signed a consent decree, a settlement enforced by the regulator. It paid a $900,000 penalty to the US Treasury, accepted a compliance plan with a named compliance director and staff training, and agreed to file pre-launch reports for three years. It then made its satellites larger and easier to track, which won it a licence, and its later commercial satellites went back to the 0.25U size. SpaceX bought the company for $524 million in 2021, told customers in September 2024 that service would end, and stopped it by March 2025.

For anyone thinking of launching from a foreign site to avoid a home regulator, this case gives a direct answer. The foreign launch did not help, because the company and its ground stations were within American reach.
swarm-spacebees-fcc.why: The 'larger satellites' sentence implied the small format was dropped; the third generation returned to 0.25U. Added compliance terms and shutdown dates.

add_sources.t: FCC Fines Swarm $900,000 for Unauthorized Smallsat Launch, Space.com

apollo-17.story:
Apollo 17 was the last crewed NASA landing on the Moon, in December 1972, in a valley called Taurus-Littrow on the southeastern rim of Mare Serenitatis. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, drove about 35.7 kilometres in a Lunar Roving Vehicle and brought back samples weighing 110.52 kilograms by one figure and about 115 kilograms by another. The descent stage of their lander Challenger, the rover and a science package remain in the valley, and no one has landed there since.

Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over its spacecraft and that landing does not change who owns them. There is no time limit. So the United States still owns the car and the rest of the hardware.

The same treaty leaves the valley unowned. Article II bars claims to land on the Moon, and the crew's stay gave no rights. The treaty does not explain how a country that cannot own the Moon comes to own rock taken from it. Countries now answer it differently. The Artemis Accords say extracting resources is not in itself a claim to territory, and the United States and Luxembourg have laws letting their companies own what they take. Russia argues that extraction creates no ownership and that one country's law cannot reach beyond its jurisdiction. Draft principles from a UN working group, in their July 2025 form, set out no rule on who owns what is taken.
apollo-17.why: Wikipedia gives about 115 kg against the 110.52 kg stated flatly. The NSSDC page could not be fetched to confirm which is NASA's.

yemeni-mars-suit.story:
In 1997 three men in Yemen, Adam Ismail, Mustafa Khalil and Abdullah al-Umari, filed a complaint against NASA with Yemen's Prosecutor General, accusing the American space agency of invading Mars. At the time NASA's Pathfinder mission and its small rover Sojourner were sending back more than 1,000 pictures from the planet. The men told the Yemeni weekly Al-Thawri that the craft had landed and begun exploring without informing them or seeking their approval. They said they had inherited Mars from their ancestors 3,000 years earlier, and they based the claim on the mythologies of the Himyaritic and Sabaean civilisations of ancient Arabia.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty had already barred countries from claiming land in space, and inheritance from ancient peoples has no place in that rule. The story comes from a popular history newsletter and Wikipedia, and no court record is known. The newsletter says the chief prosecutor rejected the petition and threatened the men with jail for wasting official time.

The claim came four years before NASA's NEAR Shoemaker probe landed on the asteroid Eros in 2001, after which Gregory Nemitz sent NASA a bill for parking there. A prosecutor in Yemen has no power over NASA or over land on Mars, and the case never reached a court.
yemeni-mars-suit.why: The four-year gap is sure only to the 2001 landing; the date of the invoice is not established.

iss-intergovernmental-agreement.why: No text change. Seven-member crew confirmed by NASA as of mid-October 2026, after Crew-12 returned on 8 October.
